hook.scenario: Your API accepts a 'discount_percentage' field. A user sends 'discount_percentage': 150. Your database accepts it, and suddenly every order is completely free.
hook.question: How do you guarantee that bad data never even reaches your business logic?

mental_model.intuition: Pydantic is a ruthless bouncer at the club door.
mental_model.description: It checks everyone's ID (data types) and applies the club rules (validators). If the payload says age=17, the bouncer rejects them with a 422 Unprocessable Entity before they even step inside your FastAPI route. Your internal code never has to worry about checking types or rules again.

sections.body: In a backend, you can't trust the data the client sends. Instead of scattering `if age < 0` checks throughout your handlers, you declare a Pydantic model. You state exactly what the data should look like using standard Python type hints. Pydantic enforces this boundary.
sections.recap: Models define the boundary: bad data bounces before your logic runs.

sections.body: Pydantic does two things: parsing and validation. Parsing means if you expect an integer and receive the string `"42"`, Pydantic silently converts it to the integer `42` (coercion). Validation means if you expect an integer and receive `"apple"`, Pydantic raises a clear validation error detailing exactly which field failed.
sections.recap: Parsing coerces types when possible; validation rejects what can't be coerced.

sections.body: Standard types aren't always enough. A string could be empty, or an integer might be out of range. Pydantic v2 uses `Field` constraints (`min_length`, `ge` for greater-than-or-equal) and the `@field_validator` decorator to enforce custom business rules directly on the data shape.
sections.recap: Use Field for simple bounds and @field_validator for custom logic.

sections.body: When a Pydantic v2 model fails validation inside FastAPI, the framework automatically catches the `ValidationError` and returns a 422 HTTP response to the client. The response body is a highly detailed JSON array explaining every single field that failed and why. You never write this error handling code yourself.
sections.recap: FastAPI + Pydantic automatically turns validation failures into 422 responses.

code_snippets.title: The naive way (no Pydantic)
code_snippets.explanation: Without a model, you have to manually check for missing keys, wrong types, and business rules. It scales poorly and makes the handler unreadable.

code_snippets.title: The realistic version (Pydantic v2)
code_snippets.explanation: Here, Pydantic v2's `Field` handles simple constraints, while `@field_validator` handles custom logic. The classmethod takes the raw value and either returns it or raises an error.

code_snippets.title: The modern v2 configuration pattern
code_snippets.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    # v2 configuration replaces the old `class Config:`
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True, extra='forbid')

    id: int
    username: str
    email: str
code_snippets.explanation: In Pydantic v2, configurations use `model_config = ConfigDict(...)`. The `from_attributes=True` setting is critical for serializers, allowing Pydantic to read fields from SQLAlchemy ORM objects (e.g. `user.id`), not just dictionaries.

key_points.title: Type Coercion
key_points.detail: Pydantic tries to convert data to the declared type (e.g., '1' to 1) before failing.

key_points.title: Field vs field_validator
key_points.detail: Use `Field(ge=0)` for standard constraints. Use `@field_validator` for custom Python logic.

key_points.title: ConfigDict over class Config
key_points.detail: Pydantic v2 configures models using the `model_config` attribute and `ConfigDict`, not the v1 inner class.

common_mistakes.title: Using Pydantic v1 idioms in modern codebases
common_mistakes.explanation: Using `@validator` or `class Config: orm_mode = True` is instantly flagged as outdated in 2026 interviews. Pydantic v2 requires `@field_validator` and `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)`.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting @classmethod on validators
common_mistakes.explanation: In Pydantic v2, `@field_validator` methods must be class methods (they take `cls` and the value), because validation runs before the instance is fully constructed.

recall_questions.q: What happens if a client sends the string "42" for a Pydantic field typed as `int`?
recall_questions.answer: Pydantic coerces (parses) the string "42" into the integer 42, and the validation succeeds.

recall_questions.q: How do you configure a Pydantic v2 model to read data from ORM objects (like SQLAlchemy) instead of just dictionaries?
recall_questions.answer: Set `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)` on the model class.
Because the validator executes on the raw input data BEFORE the actual instance of the model has been created.

oa_questions.question: A candidate's code review submission includes: `class User(BaseModel): class Config: orm_mode = True`. What is wrong with this in a modern FastAPI application?
oa_questions.answer: It uses Pydantic v1 syntax. In modern FastAPI (Pydantic v2), configurations must use `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)`.
oa_questions.approach: Identify the outdated `class Config` and `orm_mode` syntax, and provide the correct v2 `ConfigDict` equivalent.

oa_questions.question: You have a Pydantic model for user registration. How do you enforce that the 'password' and 'confirm_password' fields match?
oa_questions.answer: Use a `@model_validator(mode='after')` (or `mode='before'`) to inspect the entire model's data. A single `@field_validator` only has access to its own field, not the others.
oa_questions.approach: Explain that field validators validate single fields in isolation, whereas a model validator has access to the full payload.
